chunks: "A clock gives a digital system a shared sense of time. Logic gates take time to settle, and on the way to the right answer their outputs can glitch.
If everything updated whenever its inputs changed, you'd have races, glitches being mistaken for real data, and no way to say when a result is valid.
The clock fixes that by dividing time into cycles. Flip-flops only look at their inputs at the clock edge.
Between edges, the combinational logic is free to settle and glitch, because nobody is looking.
As long as the logic finishes inside one period, setup and hold are met, and at the next edge every flip-flop captures a clean value at the same time.
So I only have to reason about 'state now' and 'state next cycle', which is what lets us design huge systems with tools.
It also gives us pipelining, where I put registers between stages so each stage has a short path and the clock can be faster, and a way to sequence operations in a CPU or state machine.
And it's the time base for timers and communication protocols.
The costs are real though: the clock network can burn a large part of dynamic power, skew and jitter eat into timing margin, and fast edges cause EMI.
The alternative is asynchronous design with handshakes, which avoids the clock but is harder to design and verify, so most real systems use clocks, sometimes with several domains."
